  "summary": "S1 — Fact: deliver a small Python HTTP service where organisers create events with seat counts and people reserve seats; reservations must respect available capacity. The HTTP interface is the consumer entry point and intended place of use. Assumptions: one reservation request reserves one seat; the runtime does not identify or authenticate people, so it cannot enforce per-person limits; event and reservation state is shared within one service process, is visible to callers, and lasts until that process stops, so it does not persist across restarts or coordinate multiple processes. Discovery must first establish the available Python runtime and hosting environment, then determine whether they provide storage, identity or deployment capabilities; this blocks confirming the state and identity defaults and a deployment target. Discovery must also establish the runtime and test tooling before settling the HTTP contract and concurrency approach; until then, use a minimal API and protect capacity against concurrent requests. Source hints: the workspace and its runtime and tooling configuration are leads; no team, channel, internal site, private repository or owner is named, and 'organisers' and 'people' are ambiguous actor terms. S2 — Fact: include tests for the service, including event creation, reservations and capacity handling; discovery of available tooling informs the test runner, with Python's standard library as the recorded default. Exercise boundary: the repository is empty, this stage is intake only, and implementation is outside this run. The request authorizes delivery of the service for use through HTTP; no deployed target is named. In an isolated run, the source checkout remains at its snapshot until the final return, when the delivered outcome becomes visible there; an outcome in a deployed target becomes visible only after release. Any sensitive locator discovered belongs only in an authorized private store, never in committed KNOWLEDGE/."
}
